prompt:
A 38-year-old man presents with progressive bilateral leg edema and foamy urine. Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein without hematuria, urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 6.5 g/g, serum albumin is 2.2 g/dL, and creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL. He has no diabetes and takes no medications. How should this new nephrotic syndrome be evaluated and managed?

Provide a comprehensive management plan including appropriate diagnostic workup, referrals, procedures if indicated, follow-up, and actions to avoid.

rubric_items.text: Refer promptly to nephrology for evaluation of new nephrotic-range proteinuria.
Confirm and quantify proteinuria with a repeat urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or timed urine collection.
Perform urine microscopy to assess for hematuria, casts, or evidence of a mixed nephritic process.
Repeat serum creatinine, electrolytes, albumin, and complete blood count.
Obtain a fasting lipid profile.
Test for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV as secondary causes.
Obtain antinuclear antibodies and complement levels when evaluating immune-mediated causes.
Order serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation and serum free light chains when appropriate.
Test for anti-PLA2R antibodies when primary membranous nephropathy is suspected.
Discuss kidney biopsy with nephrology to establish the cause before disease-specific immunosuppression.
Assess volume status and begin sodium restriction with judicious diuretic therapy for clinically significant edema.
Assess venous thromboembolism risk and provide urgent evaluation instructions for symptoms of thrombosis.
Start high-dose immunosuppression before establishing the cause of nephrotic syndrome.
Dismiss the proteinuria because serum creatinine is normal.
Treat the edema with unrestricted high-dose diuretics without monitoring volume status, creatinine, or electrolytes.
Recommend a high-sodium diet.
Begin full-dose anticoagulation automatically without individualized thrombosis and bleeding assessment.
Delay nephrology referral until kidney function declines.
Order cystoscopy as the primary evaluation despite absent hematuria.
Attribute the proteinuria to diabetes despite no history or evidence of diabetes.
Recommend severe dietary protein restriction, such as 0.3–0.4 g/kg/day without specialist nutritional support, in this patient with preserved kidney function.
Administer intravenous albumin routinely without a specific indication or monitoring.
Start an aminoglycoside antibiotic for the proteinuria.
Advise the patient to ignore new unilateral leg swelling, chest pain, or dyspnea.
Initiate an ACE inhibitor or ARB for hypertension and proteinuria after assessing volume status and contraindications.
Arrange follow-up to reassess blood pressure, weight, and edema, and check creatinine and potassium within 2–4 weeks of starting or titrating an ACE inhibitor, ARB, or diuretic.
